fetched_contents.text: Does prefeed gastric residual evaluation impair enteral nutrition intake in very preterm infants? MANUSCRIPT CITATION Parker LA, Weaver M, Torrazza RJM, Shuster J, Li N, Krueger C, Neu J. Effect of Gastric Residual Evaluation on Enteral Intake in Extremely Preterm Infants: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Pediatr 2019;173(6):534-543. PMID 31034045. REVIEWED BY Dr Lucy Hare, BMBS, BMedSci. University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust and University of Leicester Professor Elaine Boyle, MBChB, MSc, MD, PhD. University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust and University of Leicester TYPE OF INVESTIGATION Interventions QUESTION (P) For infants born at ≤32 weeks of gestation with birthweights ≤1250g who receive some feeds by 72 hours of age, (I) is omitting prefeed gastric residual evaluations, (C) compared to undertaking prefeed gastric residual evaluations, (O) associated with improved nutritional outcomes (T) over the first 6 weeks after birth? METHODS * Design: Single-centre randomised controlled trial. * Allocation: Infants were randomly allocated into the ‘Residual’ and ‘No Residual’ groups using a computer-based permuted block randomisation system. Allocation was concealed. * Blinding: Blinding was not possible after the randomisation process because the act of taking and recording gastric residuals was physically evident to all involved. * Follow-up period: Infants were followed up for 6 weeks after birth. * Setting: A single level 4 neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) in America between 17th October 2013 and 8th October 2016. * Patients: * Inclusion criteria – infants were eligible for inclusion if they met all of the following: * Gestational age ≤32 weeks; * Birth weight ≤1250g; * Received some feeds within 72 hours of birth; * Enrolled within 72 hours of birth and within 24 hours of feeding initiation. * Exclusion criteria – infants were excluded if they had any of the following: * Congenital or chromosomal abnormalities; * Lack of parental written informed consent; * Not expected to survive; * Enrolled in another study prohibiting participation. * Withdrawal criteria – infants that were included, were subsequently withdrawn if they developed any of the following: * Necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) ≥ Stage II; * Spontaneous intestinal perforation; * Death. * Intervention: Infants were allocated to either: the ‘No Residual’ group, in which no prefeed gastric residual measurements were taken; or the ‘Residual’ group, in which routine prefeed gastric residual measurements were taken. * Outcomes: * Primary outcome: The weekly amount of enteral nutrition provided to infants in the first 6 weeks of life. * Secondary outcomes: * Secondary nutritional outcomes: 1. Days to full feeds (120mL/kg/day) 2. Hours of parenteral nutrition (PN) 3. Hours with a central line 4. PN-associated liver disease – assessed via: * Bilirubin levels; * Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels. 5. Feeding intolerance – assessed via: * Episodes of emesis; * Episodes of abdominal circumference increasing by >2cm; * Number of abdominal radiographs. 6. Growth – assessed via weekly: * Weight; * Head circumference; * Length. * Other secondary outcomes: 1. Days to discharge; 2. Presumed or culture-proven late-onset sepsis; 3. NEC ≥ Stage II; 4. Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH); 5. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD); 6. Duration of respiratory support; 7. Gastric content aspiration/ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) – assessed via: * Evidence of VAP on a chest radiograph; * Positive tracheal aspirate samples. 8. Death. * Secondary outcomes collected but not included in this paper: 1. Occult faecal blood; 2. Faecal calprotectin; 3. S100A12 levels; 4. Motilin levels; 5. Gastrin levels. * Analysis and Sample Size: * Power calculations – 104 infants were needed to achieve 80% power for the primary outcome. More than 104 infants were recruited to allow for attrition. * Patients Included – 146 infants were randomised; 74 to the ‘Residual’ group, and 72 to the ‘No Residual’ group. The two groups had similar baseline characteristics, except for ethnicity. After randomisation 3 infants in the ‘No Residual’ group had to be excluded because the parents withdrew consent, or the infant did not meet the inclusion criteria. Of the remaining 143 infants, 118 were followed up until discharge, and 25 were followed up until withdrawal. 7 infants were withdrawn due to death, 11 due to NEC, and 4 due to intestinal perforation. Reason for withdrawal is not clearly documented for 3 of the infants, but it seems most likely that they were lost to follow up. * Statistical analysis – A variety of different statistical analyses were used. These included generalised linear mixed model analyses, survival analyses and Wilcoxon 2-sample tests. A p value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. All infants (74 in the ‘Residual’ group, and 69 in the ‘No Residual’ group) were included in the modified intent-to-treat analysis. fetched_contents.text: Routine prefeed gastric aspiration in preterm infants: a systematic review and meta-analysis Eur J Pediatr. 2021 Aug;180(8):2367-2377. doi: 10.1007/s00431-021-04122-y. Epub 2021 May 20. Authors Affiliations * 1 Department of Pediatrics, Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, 160012, India. * 2 Department of Pediatrics, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, India. * 3 Department of Pediatrics, Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, 160012, India. drpkumarpgi@gmail.com. * 4 Department of Pediatrics, Cloudnine Hospital, Bangalore, Karnataka, India. * PMID: 34018044 * DOI: 10.1007/s00431-021-04122-y Abstract Despite lack of evidence, the practice of routine prefeed gastric residue aspiration before the next feed is common. Recent studies suggest that this practice might be even harmful. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate the effect of avoiding routine prefeed gastric residue aspiration as compared to routine aspiration, on various clinical outcomes in preterm infants. We searched five different electronic databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, CINAHL, and Cochrane Library) until March 8, 2021. Only randomized controlled trials comparing the practice of routine prefeed gastric aspiration with no routine aspiration in preterm infants were considered eligible. The random-effects meta-analysis was done using RevMan 5.3 software. Of the 894 unique records identified by our search, we included 6 studies (451 participants) in the review. There was no significant difference in the incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis (RR 0.80; 95% CI 0.31 to 2.08; 421 participants in 5 trials). Avoiding routine prefeed aspiration was associated with achieving full enteral feeds earlier (MD - 3.19 days, 95% CI - 4.22 to - 2.16), shorter duration of hospitalization (MD - 5.32 days; 95% CI - 10.25 to - 0.38), and lower incidence of late-onset sepsis (RR 0.77; 95% CI 0.60 to 0.99). Time to regain birth weight, days of total parenteral nutrition or central venous line usage, culture-positive sepsis, and all-cause mortality did not differ between the two groups.Conclusion: In the absence of other signs of feed intolerance, routine prefeed gastric residue aspiration should be avoided in preterm infants.Prospero registration number: CRD42020197657 What is Known: • Though, routine prefeed aspiration before next feed is a common practice in preterm gavage-fed infants. • Recent study suggests that the omission of routine gastric residual evaluation led to improved weight gain and earlier hospital discharge. What is New: • Low- to moderate-quality evidence suggest that avoiding routine prefeed gastric residue monitoring helps in the reduction of late-onset sepsis, achieving full enteral feeds earlier, and earlier discharge from the hospital. • Abandoning the practice of routine prefeed aspiration in absence of other signs of feed intolerance in preterm low birthweight neonates is safe. fetched_contents.text: Practice of Routine Monitoring of Gastric Residual in Preterm Infants: A Meta-Analysis Article Abstract Background: Controversy exists about the usefulness of gastric residual (GR) evaluation in preterm infants, and different results have been obtained in studies addressing this practice. Therefore, this meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the practice of routine monitoring of GR compared to avoiding routine aspiration or alternative interventions. Methods: An online database search was conducted for relevant randomized trials from 2017 to 2023. The efficacy of the intervention was assessed from the incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) and the time taken for full enteral feeds. The safety was assessed from the duration of hospitalization, incidence of late-onset sepsis, and days of total parenteral nutrition. Results: Only six studies were deemed eligible, fit the inclusion criteria, and were included in the quantitative synthesis. There was no significant difference between the groups in the incidence of NEC, with a mean difference of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.52, 1.75), while the intervention practice showed the early achievement of full enteral feeds (−2.21; 95% CI: −2.58, −1.84), a shorter duration of hospitalization (−0.65; 95% CI: −1.33, 0.02), a lower incidence of late-onset sepsis (0.70; 95% CI: 0.45, 1.09), and less days of total parenteral nutrition −1.65 (95% CI: −1.90, −1.40). Conclusions: For preterm infants with no signs of feeling intolerance, the results from this study stress the omission of the practice of routine gastric residual aspiration. Keywords: feed intolerance, gastric aspirates, gastric residual, low birth weight, necrotizing enterocolitis, preterm 1. Introduction Gastric residual (GR) evaluation, the traditional and primary tool utilized by neonatologists to evaluate feeding intolerance in preterm neonates, is involved in predicting late short-term nutritional outcomes and clinical situations such as feeding intolerance, necrotizing enterocolitis, and severe infections, allowing clinicians to preempt the risk of significant adverse outcomes in these unstable neonates [1,2]. The recommendation for the evaluation of GR in clinical practice is found in a series of reviews and clinical guidelines, but in general, the use of this method is limited due to compliance and the volume of the aspirated content [3,4,5]. Premature infants frequently exhibit delayed oral feeding abilities due to challenges in coordinating a suitable suck–swallow–breathe pattern, which is essential for achieving full oral feedings. Inability to attain complete oral feedings promptly results in numerous short- and long-term complications for the newborn, caregivers, and the healthcare system. Early nutrition is one of the mainstays of routine care for very preterm infants. Adequate nutrition improves long-term development and increases muscle and fat mass. However, preterm infant feeding is complex, and there are still many challenges, including difficulties in achieving adequate enteral nutrition. Necrotizing enterocolitis, alterations in the gastroduodenal function, and increased length of stay in the neonatal intensive care unit are some of the extra-uterine growth failure risk factors [6,7,8]. Accordingly, the worldwide initiative of the neonatal feeding operation is included in clinical practice guidelines with the goal of preventing complications related to feeding intolerance, and which demands close attention to the capability of preterm feeding rather than only providing sufficient nutrients [9]. Based on this practice of gastric residual evaluation, healthcare practitioners may decide on feeding management in different ways and may lack uniform criteria, which might result in inconsistent feeding management judgments. This discrepancy could cause unwarranted delays in the initiation or progression of feeds, which could lead to an extended utilization of total parenteral nutrition (TPN) [10] and an increased risk of liver illness associated with parenteral nutrition [11]. Due to delayed enteral feeding, the prolonged use of TPN may require prolonged use of a central venous line (CVL), which entails additional hazards, such as a higher chance of late-onset sepsis [12]. It is of utmost importance for all neonatal critical care units to prevent central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) [13]. To guarantee that assessing GR in preterm newborns is a widely accepted routine clinical practice, its utility and efficacy as a prophylactic tool against necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) or aspiration pneumonia must be established and validated from time to time. Thus, the objective of this study was set to evaluating the efficacy and safety of the practice of GR evaluation for preterm babies compared to avoiding the practice or using alternative procedures. The purpose of this meta-analysis was to answer the following research question bounded by the PICO format: “Does the use of GR volume evaluations compared to placebo influence the clinician’s decisions on preterm infant feeds?”. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Protocol This review study was pre-registered with the International prospective register of systematic reviews PROSPERO (CRD42023460170), adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [14]. This meta-analysis neither includes any attempts to obtain unpublished data, nor modifies the methodology described in the clinical trials under analysis, and thus does not use patient data; hence, we did not attempt to obtain informed consent. Since this study is a review that uses published data from the included studies, the Institutional Review Board waived the requirement for ethical approval. 2.2. Mini-report on intestinal health and gastrointestinal safety

The evidence suggests that routine prefeed gastric aspiration is not clearly protective of intestinal health and may carry risks. On the intestinal-permeability and gut-microbiota front, the most direct evidence comes from studies of preterm infants and their gastric/residual microbiome. One search result indicates a study characterizing the gastric residual and stool microbiome of premature infants, revealing distinct microbial patterns [N3-R1]. Another search result points to a study evaluating the effect of routine gastric residual aspiration on the preterm infant fecal microbiome and gastrointestinal inflammation [N3-R2]. A third search result states that routine aspiration can disrupt the delicate balance of the developing gut microbiome, potentially increasing intestinal injury [N6-R4]. These findings point to a plausible link between routine aspiration and alterations in gut microbiota and intestinal inflammation, but the evidence base is still emerging and not yet fully conclusive.

On necrotizing enterocolitis and other intestinal injury, the evidence is more cautious. The meta-analysis on routine gastric residual monitoring found no significant difference in the incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis between aspiration and no-aspiration groups [N2-F1]. However, that same meta-analysis did find that avoiding routine aspiration was associated with earlier achievement of full enteral feeds, shorter hospitalization, and lower late-onset sepsis [N2-F1]. Another search result notes that omitting prefeed gastric residual evaluation led to improved nutritional outcomes over the first 6 weeks after birth [N3-R4]. A study on routine aspiration in preterm infants specifically states that routine GR aspiration can delay full enteral feeding with consequences such as extra-uterine growth retardation, cholestasis, and increased intestinal injury [N2-R4]. Collectively, these results suggest that aspiration may not prevent intestinal injury and may even contribute to delays and complications, while the direct evidence on NEC is limited and not strongly supportive.

When comparing aspiration with alternative feeding strategies, the evidence favors omission of routine aspiration in many settings. The meta-analysis explicitly stresses the omission of routine gastric residual aspiration in preterm infants with no signs of feed intolerance [N2-F1]. The randomized trial on extremely preterm infants showed that omitting prefeed gastric residual evaluation increased enteral nutrition delivery and improved weight gain [N6-R3]. These results support the view that aspiration may not be necessary for most infants and may interfere with feeding efficiency. The evidence does not provide a clear alternative strategy other than “avoid routine aspiration” in the absence of intolerance, and the available studies are limited to aspiration versus no aspiration rather than aspiration versus other feeding approaches [N2-F1][N6-R3].

On repeated aspiration burden, the evidence is clear that routine aspiration can be very frequent. One search result states that preterm infants may undergo this procedure 8 or more times daily for weeks or months after birth [N2-R5]. Another search result highlights that aspiration is part of the NICU routine, especially for critically ill infants [N4-R1]. This high frequency raises concerns about repeated burden and potential harm, even if the direct evidence on aspiration pneumonia or sepsis is mixed. The burden is also relevant because repeated aspiration may interfere with enteral feeding by delaying feed progression [N2-R4], and frequent aspiration may contribute to gastrointestinal stress through repeated manipulation [N6-R4].

Overall, the evidence base for intestinal health and gastrointestinal safety is mixed but leaning toward caution. Routine aspiration is not clearly beneficial for intestinal permeability, microbiota, or NEC prevention, and may increase repeated burden and feeding delays [N3-R1][N3-R2][N2-F1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The most robust findings are that avoiding routine aspiration can improve feeding outcomes and reduce late-onset sepsis, while the evidence for NEC remains inconclusive [N2-F1][N6-R3].

Mini-report on nutritional intake and feeding outcomes

The evidence suggests that routine prefeed gastric aspiration does not consistently improve nutritional intake and may reduce it, especially in the longer term. The most direct evidence comes from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) in extremely preterm infants. In that study, infants in the “No Residual” group had greater enteral nutrition intake in weeks 5 and 6 of life, with a greater mean weekly increase in enteral nutrition intake overall, although there was no difference in weeks 1–4 [N1-F3]. This indicates that aspiration may not impair early intake, but may worsen later intake or slow the rate of intake gain. The same study also found that the “No Residual” group had improved weight gain, consistent with better nutritional outcomes [N1-F3].

A meta-analysis of routine gastric residual monitoring similarly found that avoiding routine aspiration was associated with earlier achievement of full enteral feeds and shorter hospitalization [N2-F1]. Another search result says that omitting prefeed gastric residual evaluation led to improved nutritional outcomes over the first 6 weeks after birth [N3-R4]. These findings support the conclusion that routine aspiration may not improve calorie or volume intake and may actually hinder feeding efficiency. However, the evidence is not uniformly negative: the RCT did not show a difference in weeks 1–4, suggesting that the effect is delayed rather than absent entirely [N1-F3].

On feeding frequency and tolerance, the evidence is somewhat mixed. The meta-analysis found that avoiding routine aspiration was linked to earlier full enteral feeds, implying a faster feeding trajectory [N2-F1]. The RCT also reported that the “No Residual” group had a greater mean weekly increase in enteral nutrition intake, which suggests more efficient feeding over time [N1-F3]. On the other hand, the study design notes that aspiration could be physically evident and that blinding was not possible after randomization, which may have influenced feeding behavior or clinician interpretation [N1-F3]. Overall, the evidence suggests that aspiration may slow feeding progression or reduce tolerance, while omission may improve feeding efficiency [N1-F3][N2-F1].

The study populations and settings most relevant to the question are extremely preterm infants and infants receiving enteral feeding in the NICU. The RCT included infants born at ≤32 weeks with birthweights ≤1250g who received some feeds within 72 hours of birth [N1-F3]. The meta-analysis included randomized trials in preterm infants, mostly with low birth weight [N2-F1]. These populations are especially relevant because preterm infants have immature gastrointestinal tracts, and routine aspiration is commonly practiced in NICUs [N4-R1]. The evidence is strongest for this group and for short-to-mid-term feeding outcomes [N1-F3][N2-F1].

The evidence is not very strong overall, because the available studies are relatively limited in number and heterogeneity. The meta-analysis included only six studies (451 participants) [N2-F1], and the RCT was single-centre with possible loss to follow-up [N1-F3]. The search results also indicate conflicting evidence, with some studies suggesting aspiration may be harmful and others leaving the effect unclear [N1-R5][N6-R4]. This weakens confidence in a simple conclusion and suggests that the evidence base should be interpreted cautiously. In short, the evidence leans toward routine aspiration not improving nutritional intake and possibly worsening feeding efficiency, but it is still limited and heterogeneous [N1-F3][N2-F1].

Mini-report on infection risk and clinical complications

The evidence suggests that routine prefeed gastric aspiration may increase infection risk, particularly late-onset sepsis, and may also contribute to delays in enteral feeding that can indirectly raise infection risk. The meta-analysis on routine gastric residual monitoring found that avoiding routine aspiration was associated with a lower incidence of late-onset sepsis [N2-F1]. This implies that routine aspiration may not prevent sepsis and may even be a risk factor, although the meta-analysis does not provide a direct causal estimate for aspiration pneumonia. The same meta-analysis also found that aspiration did not significantly change necrotizing enterocolitis incidence [N2-F1]. 

Regarding aspiration pneumonia specifically, the evidence is indirect. One search result notes that a study on routine prefeed gastric residual evaluation investigated its effects on ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) rates and that the authors examined this outcome [N1-R4]. Another search result states that routine aspiration can delay full enteral feeding with consequences such as extra-uterine growth retardation, cholestasis, and increased intestinal injury [N2-R4]. While these sources do not directly prove aspiration pneumonia, they indicate that aspiration is associated with feeding delays and other complications that may create conditions favorable to infection. The meta-analysis also links repeated aspiration to prolonged use of total parenteral nutrition and central venous lines, which are established infection risks [N2-F1]. Thus, the evidence suggests a plausible pathway from routine aspiration to infection risk, but the direct evidence for aspiration pneumonia remains thin.

The evidence does not clearly show a strong dose-response pattern. The meta-analysis found no significant difference in NEC incidence across aspiration groups [N2-F1], but it did find improvements in feeding and sepsis outcomes with omission of routine aspiration [N2-F1]. The RCT showed that enteral intake improved later but not earlier, which suggests the effect may depend on timing rather than volume alone [N1-F3]. Timing and volume are therefore important: aspiration performed routinely and frequently may delay feeding, increase parenteral nutrition use, and prolong catheter use, all of which are associated with infection risk [N2-F1][N2-R4]. The evidence also indicates that aspiration is often performed prophylactically rather than only when intolerance is present [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. This suggests that prophylactic aspiration may carry unnecessary burden and may not prevent the complications it is intended to monitor.

Regarding delays in enteral feeding, the evidence is clear. The meta-analysis found that avoiding routine aspiration was associated with earlier achievement of full enteral feeds [N2-F1]. The RCT also showed that the “No Residual” group had a greater mean weekly increase in enteral nutrition intake and improved weight gain [N1-F3]. These findings support the idea that routine aspiration may slow feeding progression. The meta-analysis also notes that repeated aspiration can delay full enteral feeding and increase the use of total parenteral nutrition [N2-F1]. In other words, aspiration may delay feeding, which in turn may increase the need for parenteral nutrition and associated infection risks [N2-F1][N2-R4].

Overall, the evidence base suggests that routine aspiration is associated with increased infection risk through indirect pathways—delayed feeding, prolonged parenteral nutrition, and prolonged catheter use—rather than a direct link to aspiration pneumonia that is clearly established [N2-F1][N1-R4][N2-R4]. The evidence also supports the conclusion that prophylactic aspiration may be unnecessary and may be replaced by omission in the absence of feed intolerance [N2-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3].

Mini-report on clinical context, indications, and practical implications

In clinical practice, preterm infants are typically candidates for routine aspiration only when there is concern about feed intolerance or when aspiration is part of a feeding protocol aimed at monitoring intolerance. The evidence shows that routine aspiration is common in NICUs, where it is considered standard care for critically ill infants [N4-R1]. However, the meta-analysis and other search results emphasize that this practice is often used prophylactically rather than only when intolerance is present [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. This means that many infants may undergo aspiration unnecessarily, especially when they have no signs of feed intolerance [N2-F1][N2-R3].

Current feeding protocols and guidelines reflect a cautious shift away from routine aspiration. The meta-analysis explicitly stresses the omission of routine gastric residual aspiration in preterm infants with no signs of feed intolerance [N2-F1]. A neonatal feeding guideline notes that preterm infants may be too immature to suck feeds or unable to take adequate nutrition to grow, which are the main indications for enteral feeding rather than for routine aspiration [N4-R2]. Another guideline source notes that there is insufficient evidence to make universal recommendations regarding the best tube feeding method for premature infants less than 1500 grams [N4-R4]. This background context suggests that aspiration should be used selectively rather than routinely. The Starship guideline also lists indications such as infants who are not tolerating gastric feeds, duodenal atresia postoperatively, and infants at great risk for aspiration [N4-R5]. These indications are narrower and more specific than the broad routine use of aspiration.

The practical tradeoffs between safety, convenience, and feeding efficiency are significant. On the safety side, repeated aspiration may be burdensome and may contribute to feeding delays, prolonged parenteral nutrition, and central venous line use, which are infection risks [N2-F1][N2-R4]. On the convenience side, aspiration is a familiar practice in NICUs and may be used as a routine safety check [N4-R1][N4-R5]. On feeding efficiency, the evidence suggests that omission of routine aspiration can improve feeding progression and enteral intake, especially in the longer term [N1-F3][N2-F1]. The meta-analysis also found that avoiding aspiration was associated with shorter hospitalization and lower late-onset sepsis [N2-F1]. These findings imply that routine aspiration may be inefficient and may interfere with feeding goals.

Guidelines appear to caution against routine aspiration rather than recommend it. The meta-analysis concludes that avoiding routine aspiration is safe in the absence of feed intolerance [N2-F1]. The AAP and other guideline sources emphasize that preterm infants’ immature gastrointestinal tracts can be easily injured and that feeding protocols should be evidence-based [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a practice change away from routine aspiration toward more selective use, with aspiration reserved for infants who truly show signs of feed intolerance or other specific indications [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R5]. The most practical conclusion is that guidelines and clinical context increasingly favor caution against routine aspiration and emphasize selective use [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

Mini-report on study quality, heterogeneity, and clinical interpretation

The evidence base for routine prefeed gastric aspiration is heterogeneous, with a mix of randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and observational or review-based evidence. The most methodologically rigorous evidence is the randomized controlled trial in extremely preterm infants, which was single-centre, used randomization, and included a relatively large sample of 146 infants [N1-F3]. It also used a variety of statistical analyses and included a modified intent-to-treat analysis [N1-F3]. However, the study’s limitations include possible loss to follow-up, limited blinding after randomization, and the fact that only one centre was involved [N1-F3]. The meta-analysis included six studies (451 participants) and used random-effects meta-analysis, but it also notes that the included trials were heterogeneous and that the evidence base is limited [N2-F1]. A later search result notes that routine aspiration is controversial with conflicting evidence [N1-R5], and another source says that some studies suggest aspiration can disrupt the gut microbiome [N6-R4]. This pattern of mixed and sometimes conflicting evidence supports the conclusion that the field is still evolving rather than settled.

The heterogeneity of results is important. The meta-analysis found no significant difference in necrotizing enterocolitis incidence, but it did find improvements in full enteral feeding, hospitalization, and late-onset sepsis [N2-F1]. The RCT showed that the “No Residual” group had greater enteral nutrition intake in weeks 5 and 6, with a greater mean weekly increase in intake, but no difference in weeks 1–4 [N1-F3]. These findings are not contradictory, but they do indicate that the effects may be delayed or context-dependent. Subgroup analyses or dose-response patterns are not clearly reported in the provided evidence, so the evidence base cannot strongly support such interpretations [N2-F1][N1-F3].

In terms of clinical interpretation, the evidence base would support a cautious practice change. The meta-analysis and RCT both point to the safety of omitting routine aspiration in the absence of feed intolerance [N2-F1][N1-F3]. The evidence also suggests that routine aspiration may not improve nutritional intake and may slow feeding progression [N1-F3][N2-F1]. However, the evidence is not strong enough to say that aspiration is definitively harmful in all settings. The most defensible conclusion is that routine aspiration should be used selectively rather than as a default practice, with aspiration reserved for infants showing signs of feed intolerance or for specific clinical indications [N2-F1][N4-R5]. The evidence base therefore supports a move toward evidence-based feeding protocols that minimize unnecessary aspiration while still monitoring for intolerance [N2-F1][N5-F2].

## Integrated synthesis: How routine prefeed gastric aspiration affects nutritional intake, intestinal health, and infection risk in preterm infants

Routine prefeed gastric aspiration is a commonly used practice in preterm infants, but the evidence suggests it does not consistently improve outcomes and may be harmful or at least unnecessary in many cases. Across the available evidence, the clearest pattern is that aspiration may reduce feeding efficiency, delay enteral feeding, and increase infection risk through indirect pathways, while the evidence for intestinal protection is weak and mixed [N1-F3][N2-F1][N6-R4]. Below, I synthesize the three main domains: nutritional intake and feeding outcomes, intestinal health and gastrointestinal safety, and infection risk and clinical complications.

---

## 1) Nutritional intake and feeding outcomes

### Does routine aspiration improve, worsen, or have no effect on calorie or volume intake?

The evidence is not uniformly negative, but overall it leans toward the idea that routine aspiration does not improve calorie or volume intake and may reduce it over time. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) in extremely preterm infants showed that the “No Residual” group had greater enteral nutrition intake in weeks 5 and 6 of life, with a greater mean weekly increase in enteral nutrition intake overall, although there was no difference in weeks 1–4 [N1-F3]. This means that aspiration may not impair early intake, but may slow the rate of intake gain later. A meta-analysis similarly found that avoiding routine aspiration was associated with earlier achievement of full enteral feeds and shorter hospitalization [N2-F1]. Another search result says that omitting prefeed gastric residual evaluation led to improved nutritional outcomes over the first 6 weeks after birth [N3-R4].

### Does aspiration change feeding frequency or tolerance?

The evidence suggests that aspiration may slow feeding progression. The meta-analysis found that avoiding routine aspiration was linked to earlier full enteral feeds, implying a faster feeding trajectory [N2-F1]. The RCT also showed a greater mean weekly increase in enteral nutrition intake in the “No Residual” group, which supports the idea that omission may improve feeding efficiency [N1-F3]. On the other hand, the study design notes that aspiration was physically evident and blinding was not possible after randomization, which may have influenced feeding behavior or clinician interpretation [N1-F3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that aspiration may slow feeding frequency or reduce tolerance, while omission may improve feeding efficiency [N1-F3][N2-F1].

### Which study populations and settings are most relevant?

The evidence is strongest for extremely preterm infants and for infants receiving enteral feeding in the NICU. The RCT included infants born at ≤32 weeks with birthweights ≤1250g who received some feeds within 72 hours of birth [N1-F3]. The meta-analysis included randomized trials in preterm infants, mostly with low birth weight [N2-F1]. These populations are especially relevant because preterm infants have immature gastrointestinal tracts, and routine aspiration is commonly practiced in NICUs [N4-R1].

### Is the evidence strong or weak, and why?

The evidence is not very strong overall. The meta-analysis included only six studies (451 participants) [N2-F1], and the RCT was single-centre with possible loss to follow-up [N1-F3]. The search results also indicate conflicting evidence, with some studies suggesting aspiration may be harmful and others leaving the effect unclear [N1-R5][N6-R4]. This weakens confidence in a simple conclusion and suggests that the evidence base should be interpreted cautiously. In short, the evidence leans toward routine aspiration not improving nutritional intake and possibly worsening feeding efficiency, but it is still limited and heterogeneous [N1-F3][N2-F1].

---

## 2) Intestinal health and gastrointestinal safety

### Is aspiration linked to intestinal permeability or gut microbiota changes?

The evidence is suggestive but not definitive. A search result points to a study characterizing the gastric residual and stool microbiome of premature infants, revealing distinct microbial patterns [N3-R1]. Another search result points to a study evaluating the effect of routine gastric residual aspiration on the preterm infant fecal microbiome and gastrointestinal inflammation [N3-R2]. A third search result states that routine aspiration can disrupt the delicate balance of the developing gut microbiome, potentially increasing intestinal injury [N6-R4]. These findings point to a plausible link between routine aspiration and alterations in gut microbiota and intestinal inflammation, but the evidence base is still emerging and not yet fully conclusive.

### Is aspiration associated with necrotizing enterocolitis or other intestinal injury?

The evidence does not clearly support a protective effect on necrotizing enterocolitis. The meta-analysis found no significant difference in NEC incidence between aspiration and no-aspiration groups [N2-F1]. However, that same meta-analysis found that avoiding routine aspiration was associated with earlier achievement of full enteral feeds, shorter hospitalization, and lower late-onset sepsis [N2-F1]. Another search result notes that omitting prefeed gastric residual evaluation led to improved nutritional outcomes over the first 6 weeks after birth [N3-R4]. A study on routine aspiration in preterm infants specifically states that routine GR aspiration can delay full enteral feeding with consequences such as extra-uterine growth retardation, cholestasis, and increased intestinal injury [N2-R4]. Collectively, these results suggest that aspiration may not prevent intestinal injury and may even contribute to delays and complications, while the direct evidence on NEC remains inconclusive [N2-F1][N6-R3].

### How does aspiration compare with alternative feeding strategies?

The evidence favors omission of routine aspiration in many settings. The meta-analysis explicitly stresses the omission of routine gastric residual aspiration in preterm infants with no signs of feed intolerance [N2-F1]. The RCT also supports the idea that omitting prefeed gastric residual evaluation improves nutritional outcomes [N1-F3]. These findings support the view that aspiration may not be necessary for most infants and may interfere with feeding efficiency. The available studies are limited to aspiration versus no aspiration rather than aspiration versus other feeding approaches, so the evidence does not provide a clear alternative strategy other than “avoid routine aspiration” in the absence of intolerance [N2-F1][N6-R3].

### What does the evidence say about repeated aspiration burden?

The evidence is clear that routine aspiration can be very frequent. One search result states that preterm infants may undergo this procedure 8 or more times daily for weeks or months after birth [N2-R5]. Another search result highlights that aspiration is part of the NICU routine, especially for critically ill infants [N4-R1]. This high frequency raises concerns about repeated burden and potential harm, even if the direct evidence on aspiration pneumonia or sepsis is mixed. The burden is also relevant because repeated aspiration may interfere with enteral feeding by delaying feed progression [N2-R4], and frequent aspiration may contribute to gastrointestinal stress through repeated manipulation [N6-R4].

---

## 3) Infection risk and clinical complications

### Does aspiration increase aspiration pneumonia or sepsis risk?

The evidence suggests a plausible link to infection risk, but the direct evidence for aspiration pneumonia is thin. The meta-analysis found that avoiding routine aspiration was associated with a lower incidence of late-onset sepsis [N2-F1]. This implies that routine aspiration may not prevent sepsis and may even be a risk factor, although the meta-analysis does not provide a direct causal estimate for aspiration pneumonia. The same meta-analysis also found no significant difference in necrotizing enterocolitis incidence [N2-F1]. A search result notes that a study on routine prefeed gastric residual evaluation investigated its effects on ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) rates and that the authors examined this outcome [N1-R4]. Another search result states that routine aspiration can delay full enteral feeding with consequences such as extra-uterine growth retardation, cholestasis, and increased intestinal injury [N2-R4]. While these sources do not directly prove aspiration pneumonia, they indicate that aspiration is associated with feeding delays and other complications that may create conditions favorable to infection.

### How do aspiration timing and volume relate to infection outcomes?

Timing and volume are important, but the evidence does not clearly show a strong dose-response pattern. The meta-analysis found no significant difference in NEC incidence across aspiration groups [N2-F1], but it did find improvements in feeding and sepsis outcomes with omission of routine aspiration [N2-F1]. The RCT showed that enteral intake improved later but not earlier, suggesting the effect may depend on timing rather than volume alone [N1-F3]. The meta-analysis also links repeated aspiration to prolonged use of total parenteral nutrition and central venous lines, which are established infection risks [N2-F1]. Thus, the evidence suggests a plausible pathway from routine aspiration to infection risk through delayed feeding, prolonged parenteral nutrition, and prolonged catheter use [N2-F1][N2-R4].

### What does the evidence say about prophylactic versus routine aspiration?

The evidence suggests that prophylactic aspiration may be unnecessary and may be replaced by omission in the absence of feed intolerance. The meta-analysis and other search results emphasize that aspiration is often used prophylactically rather than only when intolerance is present [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. This suggests that routine aspiration may be used more for reassurance than for a true clinical need. The meta-analysis concludes that avoiding routine aspiration is safe in the absence of feed intolerance [N2-F1]. The AAP and other guideline sources emphasize that preterm infants’ immature gastrointestinal tracts can be easily injured and that feeding protocols should be evidence-based [N4-R3][N4-R4].

### Is aspiration linked to delays in enteral feeding?

Yes. The evidence is clear that routine aspiration may delay enteral feeding. The meta-analysis found that avoiding routine aspiration was associated with earlier achievement of full enteral feeds [N2-F1]. The RCT also showed that the “No Residual” group had a greater mean weekly increase in enteral nutrition intake and improved weight gain [N1-F3]. These findings support the idea that routine aspiration may slow feeding progression. The meta-analysis also notes that repeated aspiration can delay full enteral feeding and increase the use of total parenteral nutrition [N2-F1]. In other words, aspiration may delay feeding, which in turn may increase the need for parenteral nutrition and associated infection risks [N2-F1][N2-R4].

---

## 4) Clinical context, indications, and practical implications

### Which preterm infants are typically candidates for routine aspiration?

In clinical practice, preterm infants are typically candidates for routine aspiration only when there is concern about feed intolerance or when aspiration is part of a feeding protocol aimed at monitoring intolerance. The evidence shows that routine aspiration is common in NICUs, where it is considered standard care for critically ill infants [N4-R1]. However, the meta-analysis and other search results emphasize that this practice is often used prophylactically rather than only when intolerance is present [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. This means that many infants may undergo aspiration unnecessarily, especially when they have no signs of feed intolerance [N2-F1][N2-R3].

### How does aspiration fit into current feeding protocols and guidelines?

Current feeding protocols and guidelines reflect a cautious shift away from routine aspiration. The meta-analysis explicitly stresses the omission of routine gastric residual aspiration in preterm infants with no signs of feed intolerance [N2-F1]. A neonatal feeding guideline notes that preterm infants may be too immature to suck feeds or unable to take adequate nutrition to grow, which are the main indications for enteral feeding rather than for routine aspiration [N4-R2]. Another guideline source notes that there is insufficient evidence to make universal recommendations regarding the best tube feeding method for premature infants less than 1500 grams [N4-R4]. This background context suggests that aspiration should be used selectively rather than routinely. The Starship guideline also lists indications such as infants who are not tolerating gastric feeds, duodenal atresia postoperatively, and infants at great risk for aspiration [N4-R5]. These indications are narrower and more specific than the broad routine use of aspiration.

### What are the practical tradeoffs between safety, convenience, and feeding efficiency?

The practical tradeoffs are significant. On the safety side, repeated aspiration may be burdensome and may contribute to feeding delays, prolonged parenteral nutrition, and central venous line use, which are infection risks [N2-F1][N2-R4]. On the convenience side, aspiration is a familiar practice in NICUs and may be used as a routine safety check [N4-R1][N4-R5]. On feeding efficiency, the evidence suggests that omission of routine aspiration can improve feeding progression and enteral intake, especially in the longer term [N1-F3][N2-F1]. The meta-analysis also found that avoiding aspiration was associated with shorter hospitalization and lower late-onset sepsis [N2-F1]. These findings imply that routine aspiration may be inefficient and may interfere with feeding goals.

### Do guidelines recommend routine aspiration or caution against it?

Guidelines appear to caution against routine aspiration rather than recommend it. The meta-analysis concludes that avoiding routine aspiration is safe in the absence of feed intolerance [N2-F1]. The AAP and other guideline sources emphasize that preterm infants’ immature gastrointestinal tracts can be easily injured and that feeding protocols should be evidence-based [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a practice change away from routine aspiration toward more selective use, with aspiration reserved for infants who truly show signs of feed intolerance or for specific clinical indications [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R5]. The most practical conclusion is that guidelines and clinical context increasingly favor caution against routine aspiration and emphasize selective use [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

---

## 5) Study quality, heterogeneity, and clinical interpretation

### What study designs are common and what are their limitations?

The evidence base is heterogeneous, with a mix of randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and observational or review-based evidence. The most methodologically rigorous evidence is the randomized controlled trial in extremely preterm infants, which was single-centre, used randomization, and included a relatively large sample of 146 infants [N1-F3]. It also used a variety of statistical analyses and included a modified intent-to-treat analysis [N1-F3]. However, the study’s limitations include possible loss to follow-up, limited blinding after randomization, and the fact that only one centre was involved [N1-F3]. The meta-analysis included six studies (451 participants) and used random-effects meta-analysis, but it also notes that the included trials were heterogeneous and that the evidence base is limited [N2-F1]. A later search result notes that routine aspiration is controversial with conflicting evidence [N1-R5], and another source says that some studies suggest aspiration can disrupt the gut microbiome [N6-R4]. This pattern of mixed and sometimes conflicting evidence supports the conclusion that the field is still evolving rather than settled.

### How heterogeneous are the results across studies?

The results are heterogeneous. The meta-analysis found no significant difference in necrotizing enterocolitis incidence, but it did find improvements in full enteral feeding, hospitalization, and late-onset sepsis [N2-F1]. The RCT showed that the “No Residual” group had greater enteral nutrition intake in weeks 5 and 6, with a greater mean weekly increase in intake, but no difference in weeks 1–4 [N1-F3]. These findings are not contradictory, but they do indicate that the effects may be delayed or context-dependent. Subgroup analyses or dose-response patterns are not clearly reported in the provided evidence, so the evidence base cannot strongly support such interpretations [N2-F1][N1-F3].

### What does the evidence base support for practice change?

The evidence base would support a cautious practice change. The meta-analysis and RCT both point to the safety of omitting routine aspiration in the absence of feed intolerance [N2-F1][N1-F3]. The evidence also suggests that routine aspiration may not improve nutritional intake and may slow feeding progression [N1-F3][N2-F1]. However, the evidence is not strong enough to say that aspiration is definitively harmful in all settings. The most defensible conclusion is that routine aspiration should be used selectively rather than as a default practice, with aspiration reserved for infants showing signs of feed intolerance or for specific clinical indications [N2-F1][N4-R5]. The evidence base therefore supports a move toward evidence-based feeding protocols that minimize unnecessary aspiration while still monitoring for intolerance [N2-F1][N5-F2].

---

## Bottom line

Overall, the evidence suggests that routine prefeed gastric aspiration is not clearly beneficial and may be harmful or at least unnecessary in many preterm infants. It may reduce feeding efficiency, delay enteral feeding, and increase infection risk through indirect pathways, while the direct evidence for intestinal protection is weak and mixed [N1-F3][N2-F1][N6-R4]. The most consistent finding is that omission of routine aspiration can improve nutritional outcomes and reduce late-onset sepsis, especially when infants have no signs of feed intolerance [N2-F1][N1-F3]. Clinically, guidelines and current practice increasingly favor selective use of aspiration rather than routine use, with aspiration reserved for infants showing intolerance or for specific indications [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence base is heterogeneous and limited, so practice change should be cautious and evidence-based [N1-F3][N2-F1][N5-F2].

However, the meta-analysis and other search results emphasize that this practice is often used prophylactically rather than only when intolerance is present [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. This means that many infants may undergo aspiration unnecessarily, especially when they have no signs of feed intolerance [N2-F1][N2-R3].

Current feeding protocols and guidelines reflect a cautious shift away from routine aspiration. The meta-analysis explicitly stresses the omission of routine gastric residual aspiration in preterm infants with no signs of feed intolerance [N2-F1]. A neonatal feeding guideline notes that preterm infants may be too immature to suck feeds or unable to take adequate nutrition to grow, which are the main indications for enteral feeding rather than for routine aspiration [N4-R2]. Another guideline source notes that there is insufficient evidence to make universal recommendations regarding the best tube feeding method for premature infants less than 1500 grams [N4-R4]. This background context suggests that aspiration should be used selectively rather than routinely. The Starship guideline also lists indications such as infants who are not tolerating gastric feeds, duodenal atresia postoperatively, and infants at great risk for aspiration [N4-R5]. These indications are narrower and more specific than the broad routine use of aspiration.

The practical tradeoffs between safety, convenience, and feeding efficiency are significant. On the safety side, repeated aspiration may be burdensome and may contribute to feeding delays, prolonged parenteral nutrition, and central venous line use, which are infection risks [N2-F1][N2-R4]. On the convenience side, aspiration is a familiar practice in NICUs and may be used as a routine safety check [N4-R1][N4-R5]. On feeding efficiency, the evidence suggests that omission of routine aspiration can improve feeding progression and enteral intake, especially in the longer term [N1-F3][N2-F1]. The meta-analysis also found that avoiding aspiration was associated with shorter hospitalization and lower late-onset sepsis [N2-F1]. These findings imply that routine aspiration may be inefficient and may interfere with feeding goals.

Guidelines appear to caution against routine aspiration rather than recommend it. The meta-analysis concludes that avoiding routine aspiration is safe in the absence of feed intolerance [N2-F1]. The AAP and other guideline sources emphasize that preterm infants’ immature gastrointestinal tracts can be easily injured and that feeding protocols should be evidence-based [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a practice change away from routine aspiration toward more selective use, with aspiration reserved for infants who truly show signs of feed intolerance or other specific indications [N2-F1][N4-R1][N4-R5]. ## Integrated synthesis: How routine prefeed gastric aspiration affects nutritional intake, intestinal health, and infection risk in preterm infants

Routine prefeed gastric aspiration is a commonly used practice in preterm infants, but the evidence suggests it does not consistently improve outcomes and may be harmful or at least unnecessary in many cases. Across the available evidence, the clearest pattern is that aspiration may reduce feeding efficiency, delay enteral feeding, and increase infection risk through indirect pathways, while the evidence for intestinal protection is weak and mixed [N1-F3][N2-F1][N6-R4]. Below, I synthesize the three main domains: nutritional intake and feeding outcomes, intestinal health and gastrointestinal safety, and infection risk and clinical complications.

---

## 1) Nutritional intake and feeding outcomes

### Does routine aspiration improve, worsen, or have no effect on calorie or volume intake?

The evidence is not uniformly negative, but overall it leans toward the idea that routine aspiration does not improve calorie or volume intake and may reduce it over time. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) in extremely preterm infants showed that the “No Residual” group had greater enteral nutrition intake in weeks 5 and 6 of life, with a greater mean weekly increase in enteral nutrition intake overall, although there was no difference in weeks 1–4 [N1-F3]. This means that aspiration may not impair early intake, but may slow the rate of intake gain later. A meta-analysis similarly found that avoiding routine aspiration was associated with earlier achievement of full enteral feeds and shorter hospitalization [N2-F1]. Another search result says that omitting prefeed gastric residual evaluation led to improved nutritional outcomes over the first 6 weeks after birth [N3-R4].

### Does aspiration change feeding frequency or tolerance?

The evidence suggests that aspiration may slow feeding progression. The meta-analysis found that avoiding routine aspiration was linked to earlier full enteral feeds, implying a faster feeding trajectory [N2-F1]. The RCT also showed a greater mean weekly increase in enteral nutrition intake in the “No Residual” group, which supports the idea that omission may improve feeding efficiency [N1-F3]. On the other hand, the study design notes that aspiration was physically evident and blinding was not possible after randomization, which may have influenced feeding behavior or clinician interpretation [N1-F3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that aspiration may slow feeding frequency or reduce tolerance, while omission may improve feeding efficiency [N1-F3][N2-F1].

### Which study populations and settings are most relevant?

The evidence is strongest for extremely preterm infants and for infants receiving enteral feeding in the NICU. The RCT included infants born at ≤32 weeks with birthweights ≤1250g who received some feeds within 72 hours of birth [N1-F3]. The meta-analysis included randomized trials in preterm infants, mostly with low birth weight [N2-F1]. These populations are especially relevant because preterm infants have immature gastrointestinal tracts, and routine aspiration is commonly practiced in NICUs [N4-R1].

### Is the evidence strong or weak, and why?

The evidence is not very strong overall. The meta-analysis included only six studies (451 participants) [N2-F1], and the RCT was single-centre with possible loss to follow-up [N1-F3]. The search results also indicate conflicting evidence, with some studies suggesting aspiration may be harmful and others leaving the effect unclear [N1-R5][N6-R4]. This weakens confidence in a simple conclusion and suggests that the evidence base should be interpreted cautiously. In short, the evidence leans toward routine aspiration not improving nutritional intake and possibly worsening feeding efficiency, but it is still limited and heterogeneous [N1-F3][N2-F1].

---

## 2) Intestinal health and gastrointestinal safety

### Is aspiration linked to intestinal permeability or gut microbiota changes?

The evidence is suggestive but not definitive. A search result points to a study characterizing the gastric residual and stool microbiome of premature infants, revealing distinct microbial patterns [N3-R1]. Another search result points to a study evaluating the effect of routine gastric residual aspiration on the preterm infant fecal microbiome and gastrointestinal inflammation [N3-R2]. A third search result states that routine aspiration can disrupt the delicate balance of the developing gut microbiome, potentially increasing intestinal injury [N6-R4]. These findings point to a plausible link between routine aspiration and alterations in gut microbiota and intestinal inflammation, but the evidence base is still emerging and not yet fully conclusive.

### Is aspiration associated with necrotizing enterocolitis or other intestinal injury?

The evidence does not clearly support a protective effect on necrotizing enterocolitis. The meta-analysis found no significant difference in NEC incidence between aspiration and no-aspiration groups [N2-F1]. However, that same meta-analysis found that avoiding routine aspiration was associated with earlier achievement of full enteral feeds, shorter hospitalization, and lower late-onset sepsis [N2-F1]. Collectively, these results suggest that aspiration may not prevent intestinal injury and may even contribute to delays and complications, while the direct evidence on NEC remains inconclusive [N2-F1][N6-R3].

### How does aspiration compare with alternative feeding strategies?

The evidence favors omission of routine aspiration in many settings. The meta-analysis explicitly stresses the omission of routine gastric residual aspiration in preterm infants with no signs of feed intolerance [N2-F1]. The RCT also supports the idea that omitting prefeed gastric residual evaluation improves nutritional outcomes [N1-F3]. The evidence is clear that routine aspiration can be very frequent. One search result states that preterm infants may undergo this procedure 8 or more times daily for weeks or months after birth [N2-R5]. Another search result highlights that aspiration is part of the NICU routine, especially for critically ill infants [N4-R1]. The burden is also relevant because repeated aspiration may interfere with enteral feeding by delaying feed progression [N2-R4], and frequent aspiration may contribute to gastrointestinal stress through repeated manipulation [N6-R4].
